The inspiration comes from Philip Ball’s argument that human social systems, viewed collectively, can mimic how nature behaves, and nature is usually described with physics. Social systems, he writes, display “collective dynamics that changes via abrupt shifts (phase transitions), metastability, critical phenomena” (Ball, 2003, p. 190); he also passes on Herbert Simon’s claim that the social sciences are in fact “the hardest sciences”, the most complex, with rules that can change adaptively over time (p. 191). The point is not that people are particles; it is that some collective patterns do not care much about the details of their parts.
The specific picture is a magnet. A piece of iron is a crowd of tiny magnets (spins), each trying to align with its neighbors while heat kicks it around and an external field pulls at everyone. The neighborhood reads the same way: each household is a spin, its decision (not its preference) is the spin’s direction, the neighbor tug is the choices of the surrounding households, the external field is norms and media and policy, and the heat kicks are random personal shocks, the punctured tire that changes today’s choice without changing the underlying preference.





3. Brock and Durlauf give the picture an economic backbone
Brock and Durlauf (2001) asked exactly the question the magnet poses: if each person slightly prefers to match the people around them, what does the group as a whole end up doing, and can more than one outcome be stable? In their framework, each individual’s utility has three parts: a private taste for the choice itself, a social part that rewards matching what others are expected to choose, and a random shock. The social part runs on a belief: one does not observe each neighbor’s decision in advance, only an expected average choice of others. Interactions can be local (a few named neighbors) or global (comparison to a neighborhood average); their paper, and this model, work with the global kind. Equilibrium is the situation where beliefs turn out to be correct, so the average people expected is the average their own choices then produce. The model borrows this whole skeleton and nothing more; no equations from the paper are needed beyond what the derivation below rebuilds.

The two arrows between worry and street are the heart of it. The fast layer is the morning: given today’s worry, parents settle immediately. The slow layer is the span of weeks: the worry drifts a small step \(\varepsilon\) toward what the street shows. Everything else in the model is bookkeeping around this loop.


5. The model, from one parent’s rule to two destinies

PresentationDetailed


The chain in one line: one parent’s rule, then the personal tipping point, then counting the street \(F(s)\), then the worry moving by the gap, then rest at \(F(s)=s\) with three crossings, then outside pressure sliding the curve left, then the walking world vanishing.

Assumptions first (they carry the equations): everyone holds a belief about the average choice of others, not per-neighbor predictions; decisions are simultaneous, with incomplete information, so only after driving does the street reveal the realization; the worry \(s\) is measured as a share on purpose, so expectation and realization share one scale.
One parent: drives when \(b \cdot s > c\), that is, when \(s > c/b\). One number, the tipping point, captures the whole parent.
The street: \(F(s)\) is the share of parents whose tipping point is below \(s\). A staircase for five parents, an S-curve for hundreds, and it never decreases. The same \(s\) plays three roles: worry level, measurable share, and threshold (“I will drive if \(x\) out of \(y\) people drive”).
The slow layer: \(s_{t+1} = s_t + \varepsilon\,(F(s_t) - s_t)\), with \(\varepsilon = 0.2\) in the figures.
Rest: \(F(s) = s\), three crossings at \(s^* \approx 0.055\), \(0.500\), and \(0.945\); stable where the curve cuts the line from above, fragile where it cuts from below.
Pressure: \(b \cdot s + h > c \iff s > (c-h)/b\), so pressure is a hassle discount; the curve slides left by \(h/2\), and at \(h_c \approx 0.167\) the walking world vanishes.
The tanh bridge: \(m = 2s - 1\); the expected margin under push \(u\) works out to \(\tanh(u)\); rest becomes \(m = \tanh(\beta(h + Jm))\), the same statement as \(F(s)=s\) in margin units.







Figure 3: Plot A. Where worry can rest: the S-curve F(s) crosses the 45° line three times, and arrows show the slow drift away from the tipping point into the two worlds. Code: plot_a() in plots.py.









Figure 4: Plot B. Two destinies: neighborhoods starting at s = 0.49 and s = 0.51, indistinguishable to any survey, end in different worlds. Code: plot_b() in plots.py.









Figure 5: Plot C. The vanishing, step by step: five snapshots as pressure grows, where the shaded below-the-line stretch is the room the walking world lives in, shrinking to a point. Code: plot_c() in plots.py.









Figure 6: Plot D. Every resting point vs pressure: the walking branch (solid) and tipping-point branch (dashed) meet at h_c ≈ 0.167 and vanish, while the driving branch barely moves. Code: plot_d() in plots.py.









Figure 7: Plot E. After the vanishing: same start (s ≈ 0.05); at h = 0 the neighborhood holds forever, at h = 0.20 > h_c the worry climbs to the driving world. Code: plot_e() in plots.py.





The assumptions come first, because they carry the equations. Following Brock and Durlauf: everyone holds a belief about what others are going to do, not a prediction of each named neighbor, but an expected average choice. Decisions are made in an instant and in parallel, so no one has complete information about what each neighbor will choose; the feeling is “it seems people will drive today”, and only after driving does the street reveal the realization. The worry \(s\) is measured as a share on purpose, so that expectation and realization live on the same scale and can be compared.
One parent. On a given morning, a parent feels a push toward driving, the worry in the air \(s\) times their personal sensitivity \(b\), set against a hassle \(c\). They drive exactly when \(b \cdot s > c\), that is, when \(s > c/b\). One number, the personal tipping point \(c/b\), captures the whole parent; \(b\) and \(c\) never matter separately, only their ratio.
The street. \(F(s)\) is the share of parents whose tipping point sits below \(s\), equivalently the share driving when the worry is \(s\). With five parents it is a staircase; with hundreds it smooths into an S-shaped curve that can never go down. Note the multiple roles the same number \(s\) now plays: it is the worry level, it is a measurable share of people, and through \(F\) it acts as a threshold, “I will drive if \(x\) out of \(y\) people drive”.
The slow layer. The worry answers the street: \(s_{t+1} = s_t + \varepsilon\,(F(s_t) - s_t)\), with \(\varepsilon\) small (\(0.2\) in the figures). The gap \(F(s) - s\) is what the street shows minus what the air expects. Two speeds must not blur: the morning decision is already inside \(F\) (fast); the worry’s drift is the \(\varepsilon\)-rule (slow).
Rest, and three crossings. Worry stands still where \(F(s) = s\), on the picture where the S-curve crosses the 45° line (Figure 3). A crossing must exist: the curve starts above the line (some parents always drive) and ends below it (some never do), and a curve with no jumps must cross. For the seminar parameters (\(\beta = 1.6\), \(h = 0\), \(J = 1\)) there are three crossings: the walking world (\(s \approx 0.055\)), the driving world (\(s \approx 0.945\)), and between them the neighborhood’s tipping point (\(s = 0.5\)). The nudge test separates them: where the curve cuts the line from above, nudges die out (stable); where it cuts from below, nudges feed themselves (fragile). Figure 4 shows the consequence: two neighborhoods starting at worry 0.49 and 0.51, indistinguishable to any survey, end in different worlds.
Pressure, and the vanishing. An outside push \(h\) toward driving enters the rule as \(b \cdot s + h > c\), which rearranges to \(s > (c-h)/b\): pressure acts exactly like a discount on everyone’s hassle and slides every tipping point, hence the whole curve, to the left by \(h/2\) for the seminar curve. Between the walking world and the tipping point the curve runs below the line, and that below-the-line stretch is the room the walking world lives in; sliding left shrinks it one for one. At \(h_c \approx 0.167\) the walking crossing and the tipping point merge and vanish (Figure 5, Figure 6), and past that the worry has nowhere to rest but the driving world (Figure 7). The same erasure can come through \(c\), since a drop-off lane lowers everyone’s hassle, so an equilibrium can be killed through the field or through the curve.
The margin bridge, and where tanh comes from. The magnet tradition measures the street not by the share \(s\) but by the margin \(m\), how far ahead driving is over walking. The two facts “shares sum to one” and “their difference is the margin” give the only conversion needed: \(m = 2s - 1\), and back \(s = (m+1)/2\). The margin has a double role that I verified by hand: \(m\) as the margin between camps (\(s_{\text{drive}} - s_{\text{walk}}\)) and \(m\) as the expected average choice (the probability-weighted average of the \(+1\) and \(-1\) choices) are the same number. For parents whose mornings vary, the standard exponential-weight recipe gives \(P(\text{drive}) = e^u / (e^u + e^{-u})\) under total push \(u = \beta(h + J m)\); the expected margin \(2P - 1\) then simplifies, in three lines of algebra, to \((e^u - e^{-u})/(e^u + e^{-u})\), which is exactly \(\tanh(u)\). So tanh is not something extra: it is the expected margin under push \(u\), written short. Writing rest on the margin scale turns \(F(s) = s\) into the Brock and Durlauf self-consistency equation \(m = \tanh(\beta(h + Jm))\); the famous equation and the 45°-line picture are the same statement in two notations.
A note on the mathematical mindset. The recurring move in the whole derivation is to create a condition where two things are set equal and read off what it implies. The crossings come from setting the curve equal to the line (\(F(s) = s\)); the slide of the curve comes from asking at which new worry a parent feels the same push as before (\(h + J(2s_{\text{new}} - 1) = J(2s_{\text{old}} - 1)\), giving \(s_{\text{new}} = s_{\text{old}} - h/2J\)). Learning to ask “what if these two are equal?” before knowing why turned out to be the productive habit.





6. The code implements exactly these equations, and checks itself by hand first
The repository (research_model_toy_two-worlds-problem) is deliberately small: numpy and matplotlib only, deterministic, no seeds. model.py has five functions, each tied to one equation of the story. F(s, beta, h) is the three-step share to margin to share recipe; drift is the \(\varepsilon\)-rule; find_crossings scans for \(F(s) = s\) and classifies stable or fragile by the local steepness; h_critical searches for the pressure where the walking world vanishes; iterate_map mechanizes the hand-iteration notebook. Before drawing anything, validate() reproduces four hand-computed experiments to machine precision, and a guided tour of every function is in code_walkthrough.md.

7. Three directions forward

PresentationDetailed









Direction
The idea




Collective household (Chiappori 1988)
Brock and Durlauf assume an individual decision-maker, which is really a unitary household. The direction is to model the household as a collective, with the escort decision negotiated between members rather than set by one utility.


Emotional factor
Emotion enters through the individual parameters: closeness lowers the hassle \(c\), felt obligation raises the push \(b\). A stronger bond makes a parent readier to drive, which is where PUDO’s emotional and relational side enters the model.


Neural-network ancestry
tanh is a rescaled sigmoid, and the Ising magnet, Brock and Durlauf, and Hopfield networks are one family. Worth keeping as background literacy for now.





Collective household (Chiappori 1988). Brock and Durlauf model an individual decision-maker who responds to the neighborhood. For a household that is effectively a unitary model, one utility standing in for the whole home. The direction is to make the household decision genuinely collective: the escort trip is negotiated between members, so who drives, whose time is counted, and how bargaining power is distributed all shape the choice. This connects the neighborhood exterior (conformity) to the household interior (negotiation), the two halves of my Year-1 reading.
Emotional factor. The toy leaves each parent’s sensitivity \(b\) and hassle \(c\) as given numbers. The emotional and relational side of PUDO is where those numbers come from: closeness to the child lowers the felt hassle \(c\), and a felt obligation raises the push \(b\), so a stronger bond makes a parent readier to drive. Bringing emotion in through \(b\) and \(c\) keeps it inside the same mechanism rather than bolted on, and it reconnects the model to the emotional-first narrative the dissertation started from.
The neural-network ancestry. The tanh curve here and the sigmoid activation in neural networks are the same curve rescaled (\(\tanh(x) = 2\sigma(2x) - 1\)), and the lineage is real, not visual: Hopfield networks and Boltzmann machines are Ising and spin models with learning, the same family Brock and Durlauf borrowed from. One family tree runs from the magnet to social-interaction choice models to neural networks. I have reserved one bounded reading block for this and treat it as background literacy, not a research direction.

title: Supplementary: Network Inference from GPS Traces
text:
2 The problem in one example
Picture two office workers, Ahmad and Bob. Their phones log GPS fixes all day. Ahmad and Bob sit in the same building from nine to five, so their traces overlap for about 40 hours a week. Ahmad and Carlos meet for dinner at a quiet restaurant once a week, so their traces overlap for two hours. A survey would say that Ahmad and Carlos are friends and that Ahmad and Bob are colleagues who never speak. A method that reads only the traces must recover that answer.
Paper 1 estimates the social-interaction effect of Lee, Li and Lin (2014): a person’s yes-or-no choice, such as driving a child to school, depends on the average choice of the people in their network \(W\). The usual source of \(W\) is a survey of ties. This page covers what happens when a researcher infers \(W\) from GPS traces instead, and where the methods in the literature fall short.

Three ideas that recur
Co-stay. Ahmad stays at the restaurant from 19:00 to 21:00 and Carlos from 19:30 to 21:15. The two stays overlap for 90 minutes at one place. A co-stay is the overlap of two persons’ stays at the same place, kept when it lasts at least 5 minutes.
Shared focus. Ahmad and Bob share a workplace, and Ahmad also shares a home with a flatmate. A shared focus is a place that structures a person’s routine, here the home and the workplace. A co-stay at a shared focus says that two persons share a timetable. It says little about friendship.
Place popularity. A ramen shop near the station draws half the town at lunch. Two strangers who both eat there overlap often. The popularity of a place is its share of all visits. A measure called location entropy rises with the number of distinct visitors.


Two traps follow

Coworker trap. A method that counts co-presence ranks colleagues above friends.
Popularity trap. A method that counts co-presence ranks strangers at busy places above friends who meet at quiet ones.

4 The simulated city
Real friendships are unknown, so I build a city where I plant them. Then I can ask each method how many planted ties it finds.
The city has 150 people, 28 days and 2,277,063 GPS fixes. Each person has a home and one of 8 work sites. The city holds 225 planted friendships, and 15 percent of them sit among coworkers. Every pair of people has one of four types:



Pair type
Count




friend (not coworkers)
191


friend_coworker
34


coworker only
1,315


other
9,635



The 11,175 pairs are all pairs among 150 people. The 225 true ties are the friend and friend_coworker pairs.
The city holds the two traps by construction.

Coworker trap. The 8 work sites put 1,349 pairs (the coworker and friend_coworker pairs) in one building for about 40 hours a week. Over four weeks, coworkers shared a median of 7,685 minutes together and friends who do not work together shared 403. Any weight that grows with time together ranks colleagues first.
Popularity trap. Solo visits pick one of 12 third places (cafes, shops, parks) with weight \(1/\text{rank}\), so the top two places take 48 percent of solo visits. Friends pick a meeting place with weight \(\text{popularity}^{-0.5}\), which favours quiet places. Strangers overlap at the busy places by chance.







NoteHow the city is built (all DESIGN)





The generator builds a 10 km box from 5 January 2026 (JST). Each person has a home, one of 8 work sites and a latent trait \(z\). The generator draws the friendships with a homophily kernel on \(z\), so people with similar \(z\) befriend each other more often. Strength takes the values 1 to 5 with equal probability, and friends meet at a Poisson rate of 0.3, 0.6, 1.2, 2.0 or 3.0 times a week by strength, for 45 to 120 minutes, on weekday evenings or weekends. People work 09:00 to 17:00 on weekdays (jitter 30 minutes, 5 percent of days skipped) and make three solo visits a week to one of the 12 third places.
The report uses event-based sampling: a fix every 5 seconds while moving, at each stay start and end, and a heartbeat every 3 hours while still. Real phone loggers behave this way. At the guide defaults, the first stage finds 13,998 stays, 161 places and 35,923 co-stays in the city.
The observed attributes age_band and gender carry a share homophily_obs of \(z\) (0, 0.5 or 1; the main runs use 0.5). Methods that use attributes see only these two columns.

R1: count the overlap
R1a counts shared visits and ignores the clock. R1b adds up the minutes and the days of the co-stays.
Example. Ahmad visits a cafe 4 times and Carlos 6 times. R1a gives \(\min(4, 6) = 4\) co-occurrences, even if the visits fall on different days. Ahmad and Bob share the office for 8 hours on 5 days, so R1b gives 2,400 minutes on 5 days. Ahmad and Carlos share one dinner, so R1b gives 90 minutes on 1 day.
R1b ranks Ahmad and Bob far above Ahmad and Carlos. This is the coworker trap in its simplest form.






NoteFormula and source






R1a Cheng co-occurrence counts (SOURCED). A location is a place and a check-in is a visit. The co-occurrences of \(u\) and \(u'\) at \(l\) are \(|C_l(u,u')| = \min(n_u(l), n_{u'}(l))\) with no time window (Cheng, Pang & Zhang 2015, Definition 1, p.2). Weights: \(\text{R1a\_total} = \sum_{l \in L} \min(n_u(l), n_{u'}(l))\) and \(\text{R1a\_places} = |L|\), with \(L\) the set of shared places (p.6).
R1b co-stay minutes and days (DESIGN). The sum of dur_min over a pair’s co-stays, and the number of distinct JST dates with a co-stay. Eagle, Pentland & Lazer (2009) and Crandall et al. (2010) give no default thresholds, so R1 stays DESIGN.






R2: weight by context
R2 asks how much a shared place or a shared time says about a tie.
R2a and R2b: weight places by how few people visit them (SOURCED). A place that many different people visit says little about a tie between two of them. The weight \(e^{-H_l}\) equals \(1/n\) when \(n\) visitors make the same number of visits. A quiet cafe with 2 regular visitors gets 0.5. A ramen shop with 4 visitors gets 0.25. WL adds the weights of the places a pair shares, and WO multiplies each weight by the pair’s co-occurrence count.






NoteFormula and source





\(H_l = -\sum_u p_l(u)\log p_l(u)\), where \(p_l(u)\) is the share of visits at \(l\) by person \(u\) (Cheng et al. 2015, Definition 2, p.3). The log base is not printed, and I use the natural log. A low \(H_l\) marks a private place such as an office, so these weights favour workplaces (p.3). \[\text{WL}(u,u') = \sum_{l \in L} e^{-H_l}, \qquad \text{WO}(u,u') = \sum_{l \in L} |C_l(u,u')|\, e^{-H_l}\] (Cheng et al. 2015, p.6). Hand test: a place with 3 visits by one person and 1 by another has \(p = (0.75, 0.25)\), \(H = 0.5623\) and \(e^{-H} = 0.5699\).



R2c: reward meetings at varied times of day (SOURCED). Friends meet in the morning, at lunch and at night. Two people who meet only between 9 and 10 each day tend to be colleagues. Split the day into one-hour intervals and count the pair’s encounters in each. Counts of (2, 10, 3, 2) over four intervals give a diversity of 3.07 effective intervals. A pair that always meets in one interval scores 1. The rung gives pairs with fewer than 7 days of encounters a weight of 0.






NoteFormula and source





The day splits into intervals of \(t\) minutes. \(P_t\) is the pair’s share of encounters in interval \(t\) (Desai, Nisar & Bhardawaj 2017, Eq. 3, p.4), \(H = -\sum_t P_t \log P_t\) (Eq. 4) and \(D = e^H\) (Eq. 5). The Rényi form is \[D_q = \exp\left(\frac{\log\left(\sum_t P_t^q\right)}{1-q}\right)\] (Eqs. 6 to 8, p.6). Defaults \(t = 60\) (Table 2, p.5), at least 7 encounter days (pp.4 to 5) and \(q = 0.5\) (p.6). DESIGN: one 5-minute slot of co-stay overlap is one encounter. Hand test (Desai p.4): counts \((2, 10, 3, 2)\) give \(H = 1.1218\) and \(D = 3.07\); the Rényi forms give \(D_{0.5} = 3.5083\) and \(D_2 = 2.4701\).



R2d: reward meetings at varied places, and weight the count by place popularity (SOURCED). A pair that meets at five different places has a higher chance of a tie than a pair that meets 20 times at one. Diversity \(D\) counts the effective number of places. A pair with 10 co-occurrences at each of two places has \(D = 2\) for every order \(q\). A pair with 10 at one place and 1 at another has \(D = 1.58\) at \(q = 0.5\), close to 1 because one place dominates. \(F\) adds up the co-occurrences with each place’s weight \(e^{-H_l}\).






NoteFormula and source





For a pair with co-occurrence counts \(c_{ij,l}\) and \(f_{ij} = \sum_l c_{ij,l}\): \[D_{ij}(q) = \Big(\sum_{l:\,c_{ij,l}>0} (c_{ij,l}/f_{ij})^q\Big)^{1/(1-q)}, \qquad F_{ij} = \sum_l c_{ij,l}\, e^{-H_l}\] (Pham, Shahabi & Liu 2016, Eqs. 8 and 9, p.13; Eq. 12, p.16). Defaults \(q = 0.1\) (pp.28 to 29) and \(\tau = 60\) minutes (p.24). DESIGN: two stays co-occur when they share a place and start within \(\tau\) minutes, and each stay joins at most one co-occurrence per partner. The combined score of Eq. 14 (p.18) needs labels and is not built. Hand test: counts \((10, 0, 0, 0, 10)\) give \(D = 2\) for every \(q\); counts \((10, 1, 0, 0, 9)\) give \(D(0.5) = 2.5649\) and \(D(0.1) = 2.8880\).



R2e: PGT, three weights per meeting (SOURCED). Each meeting event gets three weights. The personal weight is large when the two people come to this spot only a few times otherwise. The global weight is small when many people visit the spot. The temporal weight is small when the meeting follows another meeting by a short time. Example: meetings on day 0, 1 and 10 get temporal weights 1, 0.18 and 0.83. A second meeting a day after the first adds little. A meeting 9 days after the previous one counts almost in full.






NoteFormula and source





A meeting event pairs two records closer than \(\delta\) in distance and \(\tau\) in time. The score is \[G(E_{ij}) = \max_k w^p_{ij}(e_k) \cdot \sum_k w^g_{ij}(e_k)\, w^t_{ij}(e_k)\] with personal weight \(w^p = -\log(\rho_i \rho_j)\), global weight \(w^g = e^{-g(loc)}\) and temporal weight \(w^t = 1 - e^{-c_t |t_k - t_{k-1}|}\) (Wang, Li & Lee 2014, Eqs. 4, 8, 11, 13 to 15, pp.3 to 5). Here \(\rho_i\) is person \(i\)’s distance-weighted share of records near the meeting spot and \(g(loc)\) is the location entropy of the spot. Defaults \(\delta = 30\) m, \(\tau = 1\) hour (p.2), \(c_d = 1.5\) per km and \(c_t = 0.2\) per day (p.8). The variants \(G_0\), \(G_2\) and \(G_3\) (Eqs. 2, 10, 12) are built. DESIGN: a meeting event joins two stays whose centroids lie within \(\delta\) and whose starts lie within \(\tau\).
\(G_1\) (SOURCED, added in S7). \(G_1(E_{ij}) = \sum_k w^p_{ij}(e_k)\), the mean personal weight times the number of meeting events (Wang et al. 2014, Eq. 9, PDF p.4). Wang et al. report that \(G_1\) is a weak separator of friends and non-friends (Fig. 2a, pp.4 to 5), so the pipeline writes it as the comparison method R2e_G1. Hand test: personal weights (2.0, 3.5, 1.0) give \(G_1 = 6.5\). A second hand test: events at days 0, 1 and 10 give \(w^t = 1, 0.1813, 0.8347\); with \(w^p = (2.0, 3.5, 1.0)\) and \(w^g = 0.2\) for all three, \(G = 3.5 \cdot 0.2 \cdot (1 + 0.1813 + 0.8347) = 1.4112\).





R3: test against chance
A null model asks how large the overlap of two people would be if each visited places at random, with the same number of visits. A small p-value marks an overlap too large for chance. The three tests differ in what they hold fixed.








Test
Holds fixed
Example in one line




R3a hypergeometric
the number of places each person visits
A town has 10 places. Ahmad visits 4, Carlos 3, and all 3 of Carlos’s places are among Ahmad’s. Random choices give that in \(7/210 = 0.033\) of draws


R3b Poisson
how many people sit in each place and time slot
A busy slot adds little to the expected co-occurrences of one pair, because many pairs share it


R3c BiCM
the number of places each person visits and the number of visitors each place has
A popular place lifts every pair’s expected overlap, so a shared visit there counts for less



R3a treats all places as interchangeable, so it does not correct for popularity. R3b and R3c do. The weight for ranking is \(-\ln p\) in all three.






NoteFormula and source





R3a hypergeometric backbone (SOURCED). With \(N\) places, \(n\) and \(K\) places visited by \(i\) and \(j\), and \(G_{ij}\) shared places, \(P(X = x) = \binom{K}{x}\binom{N-K}{n-x}/\binom{N}{n}\) and \(p = P(X \ge G_{ij})\) (Domagalski, Neal & Sagan 2021, p.5). An edge stays when \(p < \alpha/2\) (p.4) with \(\alpha = 0.01\) (pp.11 to 12) and Bonferroni over all pairs (p.11). DESIGN: one visit puts a 1 in the binary matrix. The test treats places as interchangeable (Neal 2014, PDF p.5). Hand test: \(N = 10\), \(n = 4\), \(K = 3\), \(G_{ij} = 3\) give \(p = \binom{3}{3}\binom{7}{1}/\binom{10}{4} = 7/210 = 0.0333\).
R3b Poisson segment test (SOURCED). A segment is a place and a 5-minute slot. With \(K\) segments, \(L_k\) persons in segment \(k\), \(M = \sum_k L_k\) and \(n_i\) segments of person \(i\), \[E(X_{ij}) = \frac{n_i n_j}{M(M-1)} \sum_k L_k(L_k-1), \qquad p = P(\text{Poisson}(E(X_{ij})) \ge X_{ij})\] (Liu, Yang, Liu & Ge 2017, Eqs. 3 and 4, pp.4 to 5). A link stays when \(p < 0.01/N_T\) (p.5); \(\tau = 5\) minutes (p.4). Hand test: \(K = 2\) segments with \(L = (3, 2)\), \(M = 5\), \(n_i = 2\), \(n_j = 1\) give \(E = 0.8\), \(P(X \ge 1) = 0.5507\) and \(P(X \ge 2) = 0.1912\).
R3c BiCM projection test (SOURCED, solver DESIGN). Cell probabilities \(p_{rc} = x_r y_c/(1 + x_r y_c)\) solve the degree equations (Saracco et al. 2017, Eqs. C.6 and C.7, PDF p.16). The overlap of two persons is a Poisson-Binomial sum over places with \(q_c = p_{rc}p_{r'c}\), and \(p = P(V \ge V^*)\) (Eqs. 2.5 to 2.8, PDF p.5). The false discovery rule keeps ranks up to the largest \(i\) with \(p_{(i)} \le i t/M\), \(t = 0.05\) (Eq. 2.9). DESIGN: a fixed-point solver with tolerance \(10^{-10}\) and a cap of 10,000 iterations, removal of degenerate rows and columns, and an exact dynamic programme for the tail. Hand test: four people in two pairs of identical rows over four places give \(p = 0.26171875\) for a pair that shares two places.
The three rungs use three tail and correction rules (\(\alpha/2\) with Bonferroni, \(0.01/N_T\), false discovery rate). No source compares them (gap G-504).









NoteVariants added in S7 (DESIGN)





R3a on day-parts. The artifact becomes a place in one of four JST day-parts: night 00:00 to 06:00, morning 06:00 to 12:00, afternoon 12:00 to 18:00 and evening 18:00 to 24:00, each half-open. A stay counts once in every day-part it overlaps, a stay across midnight counts on both sides, and the test ignores the date. Hand test: three people visit seven (place, day-part) artifacts, and a pair with \(n = 4\), \(K = 3\) and \(G = 2\) gets \(p = 22/35 = 0.628571\); the place-only test of the same stays gives \(p = 0.25\). The method is R3a_logp_daypart.
C11b, R3a with a gender-stratified reference. For a pair of one gender, \(N\) counts the places that at least one person of that gender visits; \(n\), \(K\) and \(G\) stay, and Bonferroni still runs over all pairs of people. A pair with mixed or missing gender keeps the full-population \(p\). Hand test: a female pair with \(n = K = 3\) and \(G = 2\) gets \(p = 0.7\) on five female places and \(p = 0.5\) on all six places, and a mixed pair gets \(p = 0.5\). The method is R3a_logp_strat.





R4 and R5: the two rungs outside the cells
R4, reconstruction with error (PENDING). R4 treats the observed co-stays as noisy views of a latent tie. Cards for Butts (2003), Young et al. (2020), Newman (2018) and Peixoto (2018) exist, and I have not verified any against the PDF, so no code exists. The card findings that matter for a later build:

Every candidate needs repeated noisy measurements of each pair, for example one co-stay indicator per day. A single count per pair is not enough.
Butts (2003) shares one error rate across all pairs, so it cannot remove the coworker trap. In a toy run, one global false-positive rate of Newman’s method absorbed shared-focus non-ties (G-503; cards unverified).

R5a, Cheng Model II (SOURCED, supervised). A logistic regression learns from pairs with known friendship. Its features are the averages over a pair’s co-locations of the maximum, minimum and mean of the time gaps between the two people’s visits, plus WL and WO (Cheng et al. 2015, pp.5 to 6). DESIGN: negatives are drawn at random, as many as ties. This rung needs labels, so it serves as a benchmark and sits outside the four cells.

8 Result 1: how well each method finds the planted ties
Three numbers describe how well a method ranks the 11,175 pairs:

AUC: the chance that a true tie picked at random scores higher than a non-tie picked at random. 0.5 is chance and 1 is perfect.
Precision at \(k\): the share of true ties among the \(k = 225\) top-ranked pairs. \(k\) equals the number of true ties, so precision and recall at \(k\) coincide.
Pair-type shares: who fills the top \(k\). This number shows the trap. A method with a decent AUC can still fill its top \(k\) with coworkers.




Pair types among the 225 top-ranked pairs of each method, with the AUC at the right end of each bar. Single city, seed 1.


The coworker trap survives every count-like weight. R1b minutes, R2d \(F\), R2e \(G\) and R3b put between 0.902 and 0.951 of their top \(k\) on coworker-only pairs and take no friend-only pair (G-300). The naive count (5-minute bins, 30 m) reaches AUC 0.774 with 0.920 coworkers in its top \(k\).
Two changes break the pattern. R2d place diversity (R2d_D_q0.1_tau30) reaches AUC 0.912 with 0.067 coworkers in its top \(k\). The shared-foci filter lifts R1b_minutes from AUC 0.837 to 0.934 and precision at \(k\) from 0.049 to 0.671. R2c temporal diversity misses its purpose here. The 7-day filter passes 1,448 pairs, and 1,349 of them are coworker or friend_coworker pairs who meet on about 20 workdays, so 0.751 of its top \(k\) are coworkers (G-304).
The null models help little. R3a and R3c score no better than the R1a count (AUC 0.694 and 0.692 against 0.694). Under their native rules they keep 8,460 (R3a), 1,357 (R3b) and 0 (R3c) of 11,175 pairs, with precision 0.026, 0.029 and undefined. Under one common false discovery rule at \(t = 0.05\) they keep 11,148, 1,360 and 0, so the choice of null model changes the edge count more than the choice of correction rule does. The shared-foci filter changes the ranking more than any null model: R3b_logp_nofoci under its native rule keeps 584 edges at precision 0.303 and recall 0.787.
R5a, trained on labels, reaches a held-out AUC of 0.781, below the best unsupervised methods on the same pairs (0.934 for R1b_minutes_nofoci).

The experiment draws choices on the true \(W\) with \(\gamma = 0.5\), then fits the model on each inferred \(W\). The covariates are an intercept, the standardised distance from the detected home to the city centre, and an indicator for age band 20 to 29 (all DESIGN). Four measures summarise the 60 fits of one network:

Bias: the mean of \(\hat\gamma\) minus the true 0.5.
Monte Carlo standard error: the spread of \(\hat\gamma\) over the fits, divided by the square root of the number of fits. A bias within two Monte Carlo standard errors of 0 cannot be told from zero.
Coverage: the share of 95 percent intervals that contain 0.5. A sound interval covers 0.95 of the time.
Rejection at \(\gamma = 0\): a second experiment sets the true \(\gamma\) to 0 and counts how often the test claims an effect. A sound 5 percent test rejects about 5 percent of the time.



Two tests for \(\gamma\)
The Wald test divides \(\hat\gamma\) by its standard error. A fit with \(\hat\gamma = 0.9\) and a standard error of 0.3 gives \(0.9/0.3 = 3\), above 1.96, so it rejects \(\gamma = 0\). The likelihood ratio (LR) test fixes \(\gamma\) at 0, refits the other parameters and compares the two log-likelihoods. A drop below 1.92 keeps \(\gamma = 0\). The standard error enters the Wald test and not the LR test, so a poor standard error cannot distort the LR test.






NoteFormula and source (DESIGN, guide v1.4)






Fixed-gamma fit. Maximise the log-likelihood over \(\alpha\) and \(\delta\) with \(\gamma\) held at \(g_0\).
LR test. \(LR = 2(\ell_{full} - \ell_{fixed})\). Reject at the 5 percent level when \(LR > \chi^2_{0.95}(1) = 3.8415\). The test of \(g_0 = 0\) gives the rejection share at \(\gamma = 0\). The test of \(g_0 = \gamma_{true}\) gives coverage: the profile-likelihood interval holds \(\gamma_{true}\) if and only if \(LR \le 3.8415\).
Failed fits. An LR column counts a fit only when both optimiser runs report convergence 0.
Out-of-bound flag. \(\text{oob} = |\hat\gamma| \ge \text{bound}\), with the bound from the contraction check on the \(W\) of the fit.
Hand test. \(\ell_{full} = -95.20\) and \(\ell_{fixed} = -97.50\) give \(LR = 4.60\), \(p = 0.03197\) and a rejection.






Out-of-bound fits
The model of Lee, Li and Lin has a unique solution only when \(|\gamma|\) stays below a bound. For a row-normalised \(W\) the bound is 1 (Lee et al. 2014 need it for a unique equilibrium of the beliefs). An estimate with \(|\hat\gamma| \ge 1\) lies outside the region where the model is defined. Such fits carry standard errors near zero, so the Wald test rejects \(\gamma = 0\) on them with ease. Example: a fit on network C10 returned \(\hat\gamma = 1.097\) with a standard error of 0.0024, a Wald statistic of 451, while the LR statistic was 2.12 and kept \(\gamma = 0\) (G-600, seed 1 of the 60-seed run). The summary column oob_share reports the share of such fits, and the experiment drops none of them.

text:
10 Result 3: what missed and false ties do to the estimate
Better friend recovery did not reduce the bias of \(\hat\gamma\) in Result 2. That raises a question: how much do missed ties and false ties in \(W\) shift the estimate? The perturbation experiment (S8, DESIGN, exploratory) answers it on the true network.
Example. The true network has 10 ties. Keep 8 of them (recall \(r = 0.8\)) and add 2 false ties (precision \(p = 0.8\), since 8 of the 10 ties are true). Simulate the choices on the true \(W\), estimate \(\gamma\) on the damaged \(W\), and read the bias. Repeating this over a grid of \(r\) and \(p\) maps the bias of \(\hat\gamma\) against the quality of \(W\). The experiment treats errors in \(W\) as measurement error for Paper 1. It does not compare methods that generate the network, which is the question of Paper 2.






NoteDesign (DESIGN, guide v1.4)






Kept ties. Keep each true tie with probability \(r\) (recall), one draw per tie. Let \(k\) be the number kept.
False ties. Add \(m = \text{round}(k(1-p)/p)\) ties, where \(p\) is the precision of the perturbed set. Draw them without replacement from non-tie pairs. With the source random the pool is every non-tie pair. With the source coworker the pool is the coworker-only pairs.
Grid. \(r \in \{1, 0.8, 0.6\}\), \(p \in \{1, 0.8, 0.6\}\), two false-tie sources. At \(p = 1\) no false tie exists, so the grid holds 15 distinct specs; \(r = 1, p = 1\) is the true \(W\).
Seeds. The perturbation draw uses seed \(10000 + s\). The outcome draw uses seed \(s\) on the true \(W\), so the choices are the same in every spec.
Hand test. \(k = 8\) and \(p = 0.8\) give \(m = 2\). Ten true ties with \(r = 1\) and \(p = 0.5\) keep all 10 and add 10 false pairs.







Bias of the estimate of the social effect at true gamma = 0.5 against the recall r of W, one line per precision p, for false ties drawn at random and from coworker pairs. The four cells of Result 1 sit at precision 0.30 to 0.32. Cells: 60 seeds. Specs: 30 seeds, so the true W (r1_p1) reads -0.059 here against -0.030 in the 60-seed table. Exploratory.


Missed ties move the bias little. At precision 1, the bias reads -0.059 at recall 1, -0.021 at recall 0.8 and -0.165 at recall 0.6, and the Monte Carlo standard errors (0.11 to 0.15) are as large as the differences. False ties move it more. At recall 1, random false ties give -0.200 at precision 0.8 and -0.262 at precision 0.6, and coworker false ties give +0.006 and -0.498. The largest bias, -0.648 (Monte Carlo standard error 0.141), sits at recall 0.8 and precision 0.6 with coworker false ties. When 40 percent of the ties in \(W\) are false, and most of all when the false ties join coworkers, \(\hat\gamma\) falls well below 0.5.
The grid shows no smooth trend, and with 30 seeds neighbouring specs cannot be ranked. The 3-seed smoke run of 5 November showed positive biases in several specs, and the sign flips with 30 seeds. The Wald intervals cover 0.50 to 0.82 of the time across specs and the LR interval 0.80 to 0.93. Between 0.20 and 0.43 of the fits fall out of bound, and the true \(W\) sits at the low end of that range (0.20).
The four cells of Result 1 show a bias of -0.284 to -0.455, the size of the specs at precision 0.6. Their precision is lower still, 0.30 to 0.32 at recall 0.72 to 0.81, and the grid stops at 0.6 (G-800). The grid cannot say whether the bias of the cells comes from low precision.

Each gap names its kind, its evidence and a strength: supported (a number or a page shows it), suggested (one run or one reading points to it) or speculative (an inference from the design). Gap ids refer to the gap log in the repository (docs/gap-log.md).

title: Supplementary: Network Inference from GPS Traces
text:
12 Limits
What the simulated city does not test. The city has twelve third places that almost everyone visits. Every pair shares at least one place (G-303), so a binary co-visit carries no tie information, and R3a and R3c have no power there (G-301, G-305). Real data has many places, so these two rungs get their fair test on real data. The home and work places are clean: R0.g finds them for all 150 people, so the shared-foci filter meets no error in them. Each person has one workplace and one home, attributes do not shape where people go, and nobody moves house or changes job. Every result is one city of 150 people; the estimation results use 60 seeds of the choice draw on that one city.
What the sources do not state. The gap-stay rule R0.b has no source (G-001, G-500). Neal (2014) and Domagalski et al. (2021) print tail rules that differ by a factor of two for the same test (G-501). No source compares the three correction rules of R3 (G-504) or states how to combine a GPS score with coarse attributes without labelled ties (G-004). The co-occurrence definitions of R2c, R2d and R2e on stays, the R0 fill-ins, the shared-foci filter, the similarity multiplier and the choice of top 5 for \(W\) are DESIGN.

Links or relationship between one person to another in a specific settings


GPS Data

Title and abstract screening
First pass over the records: I read only the title and abstract and mark each record include, unsure or exclude.


Full text screening
Second pass: I read the whole paper and decide whether it meets the inclusion criteria of the review.


Citation chaining
Finding further papers by following the reference lists of known papers (backward) and the papers that cite them (forward).


Filter rules
Fixed rules that remove records before anyone reads them, for example by document type, language or missing key words. Every removed record stays in the sheet with its reason.


PRISMA 2020
A reporting guideline for systematic reviews. It lists what a review should report, such as the sources searched, the screening method and a flow diagram of record counts.


Cohen’s kappa
A measure of agreement between two screening passes that removes the agreement expected by chance. 1 is perfect agreement and 0 is chance level.


Shared visit (co-location)
Two people recorded at the same place in the same time window.


Proximity versus friendship
Proximity means two people are near each other. Friendship needs more, because coworkers share a place every day without being friends.


Stochastic actor-based model
A model of how a network changes over time: each person adds, keeps or drops ties in small steps, and the model estimates the rules behind those choices.

text:
3. Definitions of Terms







Term
Definition




Weights matrix \(W\) (or \(G\))
The network, written as a table: row \(i\), column \(j\) holds \(w_{ij}\), how much household \(i\) weighs household \(j\)’s belief. Row-normalized so each row sums to 1; \(w_{ii}=0\).


\(M_i^*\)
Household \(i\)’s equilibrium belief about the neighborhood, on the \([-1,+1]\) margin scale — the network analogue of the single shared \(m^*\) in my existing model.


\(\gamma\) (endogenous effect)
The strength of the social pull: how much a household’s belief responds to \((WM^*)_i\), its own friends’ average belief. Plays the role \(\beta J\) played in the group-average model.


Contextual effect (\(\delta\))
How much a household’s belief responds to its friends’ characteristics (e.g. their distance to school), as opposed to friends’ beliefs.


Contraction mapping
The condition guaranteeing the belief-updating map has exactly one fixed point regardless of starting guess — Banach’s theorem, distinct from mere existence of a fixed point (Brouwer’s theorem).


\(\lvert\gamma\rvert<1\)
The sufficient contraction bound used throughout Section 7: below it, the rational-expectations equilibrium is provably unique.


NFXP (nested fixed-point) estimation
A maximum-likelihood estimator that re-solves the entire network equilibrium inside every likelihood evaluation, rather than approximating it. Slower but exact; the estimation method used throughout.


Group vs. network structure
Group: every member responds equally to the whole group’s average (a network where every tie has equal weight — a special case). Network: each member responds only to its own, generally distinct, set of ties.


Complete vs. incomplete information
Complete: an agent observes others’ actual choices. Incomplete: an agent only forms a belief (a rational expectation) about others’ choices, without observing them directly. My model and Lee’s are both incomplete-information.
